candidates.name: qcew-data
candidates.what_it_holds: download-data.sh + import-data.py: downloads BLS QCEW annual CSVs 1990-2015 (25 years, ~36.4 GB uncompressed) at county/MSA/state/national level, all NAICS industries incl. NAICS 72 (Accommodation & Food Services) and NAICS 71/72/812 leisure-adjacent sectors, and loads them into a Postgres/SQLAlchemy database. No data committed, pull-only.
candidates.why_useful: A one-command pull path for county- and MSA-level QCEW employment/wage counts for the accommodation/food-services supersector, which is the closest public proxy for Airbnb-adjacent hospitality labour cost and headcount trends (STR cleaning/maintenance labour cost inputs, margin cost-line context). Not in our current holdings (we hold FRED/BLS CPI series but no QCEW industry-level puller).

candidates.name: jp-qcew
candidates.what_it_holds: Pipeline (Polars/DuckDB, GPLv3, 92 commits) that reads raw fixed-width QCEW text files (2003 onward) and outputs partitioned Parquet with employment indices, total/taxable wages, and geospatial establishment coordinates by industry and geography. Development has moved to Codeberg; GitHub copy still functional as a processing reference.
candidates.why_useful: Faster QCEW-to-Parquet processing path than raw BLS text files if the team wants county-level leisure & hospitality (NAICS 70-72) employment/wage series as a labour-cost input to the margin model.

candidates.name: qcew
candidates.what_it_holds: MIT-licensed Python scripts (extract_data.py, extract_data_08_12.py) that extract data from BLS QCEW; small repo (1 star, 4 commits), no data committed.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative lightweight QCEW extraction script; marginal value over qcew-data given no data committed and minimal documentation.

candidates.name: entrydatar
candidates.what_it_holds: R package (10 stars, 117 commits) that downloads and aggregates U.S. firm-entry statistics: QCEW establishment-level entry data 1975-2016 (NAICS 1990-2016, SIC 1975-2000), Business Employment Dynamics (BED) establishment entry at 3-digit NAICS 1992Q3-2015Q1, and County Business Patterns (CBP) annual county employment. Includes vignettes for Bartik-shock construction.
candidates.why_useful: Gives establishment entry/exit rates by industry (including accommodation/food services, NAICS 72) at the county level over four decades — a possible proxy for hospitality-sector business formation/closure cycles that could contextualize STR/hotel supply growth alongside labour-cost pressure. Longer time span than anything we hold on hospitality establishment counts.

candidates.name: bls_download
candidates.what_it_holds: Python wrapper (20 commits) for the BLS Public Data API v2.0: labstat_download.py pulls any LABSTAT series by Series ID (handles the 50-series/10-sec and 20-year API constraints), qcew_download.py retrieves QCEW files, cps_download_v2.py pulls monthly CPS basic files from NBER. Generic — not restricted to any industry, so it can pull CES leisure & hospitality employment (SUAB series) and average-hourly-earnings series for NAICS 70-72 as well as QCEW industry detail. No data committed, requires free BLS API key (not a paid key).
candidates.why_useful: A ready-made, no-cost API client that could pull CES leisure & hospitality employment/wage series and QCEW industry detail on a point-in-time-friendly cadence (each pull is a snapshot), which would let the team build its own hospitality labour-cost/headcount time series to feed the margin model's COGS/opex assumptions.

candidates.name: py_BLS_ (unverified - 404 on direct fetch)
candidates.what_it_holds: Search-result snippet only: "Python Wrapper for the Bureau of Labor Statistics Public Data API", 7 stars, last updated Jan 2019. Direct WebFetch to the repo URL returned 404 (may be renamed/deleted/archived under a different path) — could not verify contents independently.
candidates.why_useful: Would be a generic BLS API client if still live; flagging for a human to re-check the exact URL (GitHub search sometimes mangles trailing-underscore repo names) rather than dropping it silently.

candidates.name: Geospatial-and-Reporting-Visualizations
candidates.what_it_holds: Maps/analysis of March 2020 QCEW employment location quotients (industry concentration) for Leisure & Hospitality and Natural Resources & Mining sectors, by county/region. 0 stars, last updated March 2021, appears to be a one-off class project map deliverable rather than a raw data file.
candidates.why_useful: Confirms Leisure & Hospitality QCEW location-quotient data exists in processed form somewhere, but this specific repo is a visualization project, not a reusable dataset or puller — low value as-is.

notes: Very sparse theme: BLS QCEW/CES leisure-and-hospitality employment and wage data, cleaning-service pricing, and STR/hotel operating-cost benchmarks are essentially absent as committed datasets on GitHub — nobody mirrors these series or builds cost-of-cleaning/STR-opex datasets in the open. What does exist is a handful of generic QCEW/BLS API pull scripts (no leisure-hospitality-specific filtering, no data committed) and one firm-entry R package with establishment-level detail by NAICS that happens to include accommodation/food services. Found nothing at all for: hotel/STR cleaning fee cost data, PPI for building cleaning/janitorial services, hospitality labor turnover/JOLTS by industry, OEWS hotel occupation wage data as a GitHub dataset, or any STR operating-cost benchmark repo (AirDNA-style cost data). Dead ends worth recording: WebSearch tool's session-wide budget (200/200) was already exhausted before I ran a single query, apparently used up by other concurrent scouts; DuckDuckGo (html. and lite. endpoints) served CAPTCHA challenges on every fetch and returned zero usable results; Bing search results via WebFetch were degraded/irrelevant (returned unrelated valve/pump/banking sites) rather than real SERPs; gh search repos hit GitHub's shared 5000/hr API rate limit twice even after a 40s sleep-and-retry. The one channel that worked reliably was WebFetch directly against github.com/search?q=...&type=repositories, though it also hit periodic 429s under concurrent scout load. Recommendation for a future pass: if this labour-cost data is wanted, the practical path is not GitHub-hosted data but a direct pull from BLS QCEW/CES/OEWS via their own API (bls_download or similar wrapper above) filtered to NAICS 71/72/812 series, since no one appears to have done this filtering and republished it as an open dataset.
